newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan aims to protect consumers in finance markets.
newsitem.headline: Japan aims to protect consumers in finance markets.

text.p: Japan's trade and finance ministries are to cooperate in drafting new consumer protection laws covering banking and financial services, ministry officials said on Tuesday.
The move, they said, was spurred by Japan's planned "Big Bang" financial reforms, which will allow banks and other financial institutions to enter each other's turf on a broad basis.
The officials said the ministries would consider measures to consolidate current consumer protection rules, which vary between banks and non-bank financial institutions.

Jurisdiction over such rules is divided between the ministries, with the Ministry of Finance (MOF) supervising commercial banks while the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) oversees credit-card companies.

"Consumer protection laws have been implemented in Europe and the United States and we need to catch up with international standards," said Hiroshi Suzuki, senior deputy director of MITI's commercial and consumer credit division.
He said consumer credit information needed to be safeguarded to make sure it was not sold through illegal channels.

The MOF official said his ministry would also consider the possibility of enacting a financial services law to protect those providing funds to financial markets, such as purchasers of bonds, although it might take several years to finalise.
"We will try to come up with measures as soon as possible, but we need to ascertain how (the overall) 'Big Bang' plan will develop," he added.
Last November, Japan announced a five-year "Big Bang" deregulation plan to liberalise its financial markets.
